title: The thinker: rounds of looking and passing notes
blurb: The thinker is the part that does the thinking. It works in rounds: it looks at the question, passes notes, and thinks again.

scenes.heading: Where we are: the thinker
caption: This is the thinker, the second part of the model. It does the thinking.
It is ours. It starts from scratch and learns only from our practice.
The planned size is about 100 million numbers. That size has never been tested.
src: architecture/FINISHED-MODEL-2026-10-09.md sec. 1 (about 100M planned) and sec. 2 (Thinker row: yes, from scratch; shape untested at 100M)

scenes.heading: Picture only: a team of note-takers
caption: Picture only. Think of a small team of note-takers sitting around one question.
Each round, every note-taker looks at the whole question again.
Then they pass notes to each other and write down what they now believe.
The same team, with the same habits, every round.

scenes.heading: Vectors: 8 control, 36 memory

The thinker keeps 8 control vectors. Two of them steer the work.
It also keeps 36 memory vectors, where its notes are kept.
Older builds had 17 vectors: 8 control and 9 memory.

scenes.heading: Control vector 0 drives the call writer
caption: After each round from round 2 on, the call writer reads control vector 0.
It either writes a request for the calculator, like sub 12 5, or writes nothing.
The numbers in the request are usually copied from the question or an earlier reply.

scenes.heading: Do controls 2 to 7 matter?
caption: Controls 2 to 7 feed no output. They only pass information along when the notes look at each other.
In an older build, switching them off at test time cost 1.6 points on the main test.
On the multi-step test they cost 7.8 points: 99.4 fell to 91.6.
Those numbers are one copy (seed 200). All six copies of that older design lost points, very unevenly.

scenes.heading: Round step 1: look at everything
caption: Each letter of the question is one box. A borrowed reader, Gemma, has already given each letter its meaning.
Each note vector looks at every letter. In later rounds it also looks at every calculator reply.
The shading inside each note is a picture only, not real numbers.

scenes.heading: Round steps 2 and 3: compare, then think
caption: Step 2: the note vectors look at each other. In code this is called self-attention.
Each note reads the other notes and keeps what matters from them.
The letters are not compared with each other inside the thinker.
Step 3: each note goes through a small network.
At the 100M step it widens to 4.8 times as many numbers, then squeezes back.
Then the notes go on to the next round.

scenes.heading: Why some questions need several rounds
caption: Tom has 12 apples, gives away 5, then buys 3. After round 2, the call writer writes sub 12 5.
It copies 12 and 5 from the question. The calculator replies 7, which is added to the notes.
Round 3 sees that reply. After it, the call writer writes add 7 3, and the calculator replies 10.
The talker, which writes the final answer, copies 10 from the last reply. A worked example, traced from the code.

scenes.heading: The bell: when to stop
caption: After each round, a tiny learned stop switch, the bell, asks: is this settled, or should it think more?
It must think at least 1 round. It can never go past 32 rounds.
It learns from a settled label: stop once no later round would have been right.

scenes.heading: Long text: is the thinker cheap?
caption: An average question has 81 letters. Every letter against every letter: 81 times 81 is 6,561 checks.
Notes look at letters instead. A rough count: 44 notes, each looking at 81 letters and 27 number slots, gives 4,752 checks per round.
Over 8 rounds, the older count, that is 4,752 times 8 = 38,016. At 81 letters, no work is saved.
Its gain is structure, not speed. By this count, much longer text would favour the notes, but that is untested.
scenes.notes: Computed by hand: 81 x 81 = 6,561; 44 x (81 + 27) = 4,752; 4,752 x 8 = 38,016 (the source says about 38,000). The 27 slots and the 8 rounds belong to the older build (calculator inside); the source calls the whole thing a rough count, nothing was run.

scenes.heading: Not known yet, and what to remember
caption: Not known: the thinker has never been tested at 100 million numbers.
Not known: whether many rounds hurt. One older probe, on one seed, found 16 rounds cost 1.2 to 1.9 points.
Experts (many small specialist networks, a few used at a time) are a separate idea, not yet tested and not covered here.
Remember: the thinker looks, passes notes and thinks, in rounds. The same blocks run every round. A learned bell is built to say when to stop.
